sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: A script is a set of instructions that automates tasks. Recognize common script extensions, automation use cases, and risks without needing to become a software developer.
sections.callout: Identify the script → automate the task → verify the result → control the risk.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Given an extension or automation scenario, identify the scripting technology, the task it can automate, and the harm a poor or malicious script can cause.

entries.title: .bat
paragraphs: Runs Windows command-line commands for simple administration, copying, drive mapping, and program launching.

entries.title: .ps1
paragraphs: PowerShell supports powerful Windows administration, configuration, information gathering, and automation.

entries.title: .vbs
paragraphs: VBScript is associated with legacy Windows scripting and administrative automation.

entries.title: .sh
paragraphs: Common Linux and Unix shell automation for files, backups, updates, and administration.

entries.title: .js
paragraphs: JavaScript is common on the web and can run in other supported scripting environments.

entries.title: .py
paragraphs: Python supports automation, data processing, administration, information gathering, and general programming.

sections.title: Use Cases for Scripting
paragraphs: Repeated, consistent tasks are strong automation candidates, but automation repeats mistakes just as efficiently as correct instructions.

sections.title: Basic Automation
paragraphs: Scripts can create folders, copy files, check systems, run commands, save time, and improve consistency.

sections.title: Restarting Machines and Remapping Network Drives
paragraphs: Scripts can coordinate maintenance restarts and map shared folders to drive letters at sign-in. Target the correct devices because restarts disrupt users and services.

sections.title: Application Installation and Automated Backups
paragraphs: Scripts can launch installers, supply options, configure applications, verify deployment, copy or archive files, send them to backup locations, and generate logs. Automated backup still requires restore testing.

sections.title: Gathering Information/Data and Initiating Updates
paragraphs: Automation can collect names, addresses, storage, processes, and installed software from many systems or start OS, application, and package updates consistently. Production updates still require change control.

sections.title: Other Considerations When Using Scripts
paragraphs: Scripts execute instructions with the permissions they receive, so review source, purpose, scope, testing, and authorization before running them.

sections.title: Unintentionally Introducing Malware
paragraphs: An untrusted script can download malware, weaken security, steal data, create persistence, or modify files.
sections.callout: Script does not mean malware, but unknown executable instructions create risk.

sections.title: Inadvertently Changing System Settings
paragraphs: A poor or incorrectly targeted script may alter networking, permissions, registry values, services, files, or accounts across many systems.
sections.callout: Understand, test, authorize, scope, and verify.

sections.title: Browser or System Crashes Due to Mishandling Resources
paragraphs: Infinite loops, excessive processes, memory consumption, storage use, or repeated network requests can degrade performance or crash browsers and systems.

sections.title: Objective 4.8 Exam Trap
bullets: Memorize the six extensions and technologies.
Automation can repeat good instructions or bad ones quickly.
A script is not inherently malware; source, content, and permissions determine risk.
Automation does not bypass testing, approval, scheduling, or rollback planning.

bullets: Map, deploy, back up, collect, or update → script
